title: Closures
subtitle: Retained lexical environments and live bindings

cards.meaning: A function that retains access to variables from its enclosing lexical scopes when executed outside those scopes. Mechanically, the function keeps a link to outer lexical environment(s); lookup still walks the scope chain, and those environments stay alive while the function is reachable.

cards.front: Is a closure only when a function returns a function?
cards.meaning: No. Returning is common, but any escaping use counts: pass to setTimeout, store on an object, export. The interesting case is when the function outlives the outer execution — not a special “inner function” type.
1 then 2. After makeCounter returns, increment still references that environment, so count stays alive. Each call mutates the same count.
cards.example: function makeCounter() { let count = 0; return function increment() { count += 1; return count; }; }

cards.front: Closure: copy values or live bindings?
cards.meaning: Live bindings, not snapshots. The closure closes over the variable slot; reads see the current value and writes update the same slot. Multiple inner functions from one outer call share those bindings.

cards.front: a reads n, b increments n; after b(); a()?
cards.meaning: 1. a sees updates made through b because both close over the same n binding.
cards.example: const { a, b } = shared(); b(); console.log(a()); // 1

cards.front: Closing over a binding vs a snapshot?
cards.meaning: Closing over a binding is not a snapshot. Snapshotting is deliberate: copy into const value = i in a per-iteration scope, or pass i as a parameter (parameters are their own bindings).
2 — same object. The binding holds a reference. Mutating properties (or arr.push) is visible to everyone who closed over that binding; reassigning the binding is a different operation.
cards.example: function hold(obj) { return () => obj; } const get = hold(data); data.n = 2; get().n // 2

cards.front: Two counters from two makeCounter() calls?
cards.meaning: Each outer call creates a new environment with its own count binding. They do not share state unless they intentionally close over the same outer binding.
cards.example: const a = makeCounter(); const b = makeCounter(); a(); a(); b(); // 1, 2, 1

cards.front: for (var i=0; i<3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0)?
cards.meaning: Logs 3, 3, 3. One function-scoped i is shared by all closures; the loop finishes synchronously with i === 3 before timeouts run; each callback reads that same live binding. Closures are working correctly. Event-loop timing decides when i is read; scope decides which binding. Pulling var i outside the for header is still 3, 3, 3.
cards.notes: Classic trap — live bindings plus shared var scope.

cards.front: Fixes for the var + setTimeout loop bug?
cards.meaning: Preferred: for (let i = 0; ...) — a fresh i binding per iteration → 0, 1, 2. Pre-ES6: IIFE (function (j) { setTimeout(() => console.log(j), 0); })(i), or a factory scheduleLog(j) / forEach callback param. Same idea: a new binding per iteration, not a snapshot of let.
cards.example: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { (function (j) { setTimeout(() => console.log(j), 0); })(i); }

cards.front: Does let in a loop work because it snapshots?
cards.meaning: No. It creates distinct bindings per iteration; each closure’s binding holds that iteration’s value.

Keep data in an outer scope only returned methods can see — factory returns object with methods that close over balance/count. Before private fields (#), this was standard encapsulation. Still common in factories and older codebases.
cards.example: createBank(initial) returns deposit/getBalance closing over balance; acct.deposit(50) // 150

cards.front: How does currying / partial apply use closures?
cards.meaning: The inner function retains the outer parameter binding. multiply(2) returns a function that still sees a === 2; double(5) is 10.
cards.example: function multiply(a) { return function (b) { return a * b; }; } const double = multiply(2); double(5); // 10

cards.front: How do memoize and debounce use closures?
cards.meaning: Memoize: the returned function and a cache Map share a closed-over binding for the lifetime of the wrapper. Debounce: repeated calls share one timer id binding so clearTimeout/setTimeout coordinate across invocations.

A callback retained an old render’s lexical environment (props/state bindings) while you expected the latest. Empty-deps useEffect + setInterval logging count forever sees the first render’s count. Fix by recreating the function when deps change, functional updates, or refs — still live bindings plus which environment the function points at, not React magic.
cards.example: useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => console.log(count), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, []);

cards.front: What stays in memory with a closure?
cards.meaning: While the function is reachable, outer environments it needs for lookup stay reachable too. Long-lived callbacks (listeners, intervals, effects without cleanup) and unbounded memo caches keep those environments forever. Engines may drop unused bindings, but do not rely on that for correctness.
cards.example: function load() { const huge = new Array(1e6).fill(0); const token = 'abc'; return function authHeader() { return `Bearer ${token}`; }; }
